courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a Gaussian: position, covariance, opacity, SH color
md: Opacity is not the alpha used in blending. Alpha at a pixel is opacity times the Gaussian's falloff $G$ at that pixel, so the same Gaussian contributes strongly at its center and almost nothing a few standard deviations away.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: LL/SC: watching the location instead of its value
md: LL/SC detects *writes*, so it is immune to A to B to A in principle. In practice the pop needs a load between LL and SC, which hardware does not guarantee to support, and languages expose CAS anyway.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Interaction effects and Shapley values
md: If two stages interact, no single number per stage tells the whole story. Test the key combinations (a 2 x 2 grid for a suspected pair), and when you need a per-stage split of the total, use Shapley values, which sum exactly to the full-minus-baseline gain.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Client-side-only checks, tampering, and trusting what the client sends
md: Client input may say *what* is being requested. Only server-side state (the session, the database, the policy) may say *whether* it is allowed. If a value that decides access can be edited in the browser, the check is broken.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Privileged groups, and why so many paths lead to Domain Admins
md: Enterprise Admins, Domain Admins and built-in Administrators each control the domain (EA the whole forest). Nesting hides membership, and every machine an admin signs in to becomes a place to steal that admin. Keep these groups nearly empty and audit them recursively.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Forged tickets: golden and silver, and the double krbtgt reset
md: Golden tickets are forged TGTs from the krbtgt key; silver tickets are forged service tickets from one service key and never touch the KDC. Detect mismatches between tickets and the KDC's own logs, and evict with two krbtgt resets after closing the attacker's access.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Watching the domain, and recovering after it falls
md: Audit the DC events that reveal each attack and ship them off the DCs. After a domain compromise, contain first, then evict every credential (krbtgt twice), remove persistence, rebuild what you cannot trust, and keep offline AD backups.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: What this means for engineers: safe languages, fuzzing, defaults
md: Prevent, then detect, then mitigate. Memory-safe languages remove bug classes; sanitizers and fuzzing catch what remains; mitigations on by default raise the cost of what slips through; and fast patching shortens the window. Every rung an attacker must climb is one you can remove.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: From one model call to an agent loop
md: The model does not execute tools. It only emits a structured request. Whether a shell command actually runs, and with what permissions, is decided entirely by harness code, which is why safety controls belong in the harness.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: The read path: scoring memories by recency, importance and relevance
md: Recency decay does not resolve conflicts. A stale fact with high importance and relevance still makes the cut, so the newer fact helps only if the reader happens to trust it more. Resolve contradictions on the write path; use scoring to choose among facts that are all still true.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: From a benchmark to an environment: reset, step and a checker
md: An agentic RL environment is a benchmark task turned into a loop you can run millions of times: `reset` to a clean sandbox, `step` per tool call, and a programmatic checker that produces the reward at the end. The simulated user in tau-bench is part of the environment, not part of the policy.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: A toy agent loop: watching a web page give orders
md: The dangerous line is never the model call. It is the loop that turns model output into actions. Put your controls there.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Model supply chain: pickle files, safetensors and signing
md: Loading a pickle is running code. Prefer safetensors, load PyTorch files with weights_only=True, and verify a signature or hash from a source you trust before loading anything.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Cheap surrogates for DFT: graph networks and interatomic potentials
md: Judge a discovery surrogate by what it does to DFT spending: precision (hit rate), recall, and DAF on unrelaxed inputs. A low regression error does not guarantee good decisions near the hull.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Distortion-free sampling: the Gumbel trick and SynthID tournaments
md: Green lists shift probabilities toward a keyed subset (distortionary). Gumbel sampling and two-competitor tournaments keep each token's distribution exact and hide the signal in correlations between chosen tokens and keyed random values. All of them need entropy to work.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Isolation Forest: anomalies split off in fewer random cuts
md: The fixed 0.5 cutoff of contamination="auto" is not calibrated to your data. In the 1000-point evaluation set of lesson 5 it flags 241 points when only 10 are anomalies. Rank by score, or set the threshold from a review budget, rather than trusting the default label.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: APIs from zero: REST, GraphQL and what a request carries
md: Misconception: "Only our app calls this API, so it is private." The app's traffic can be read and replayed by anyone who installs it, and API keys built into an app can be extracted from it. Treat every request as if a stranger typed it by hand.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Redirect URIs, the state parameter and OAuth CSRF
md: Misconception: state is optional decoration. Without state, PKCE, or nonce, any OAuth client can be logged into an attacker's account. RFC 6749 and RFC 9700 both make CSRF protection a must.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Classic JWT bugs: alg none, RS256 to HS256, kid and jku
md: Every one of these bugs is the same mistake: letting data inside the unverified token decide how the token is verified. The receiver fixes the algorithm, the key set and the audience; the token only gets to say which of the receiver's keys it used.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Design review in the cycle: deciding which changes get a threat model
md: A design review that happens after the code is written is an audit, not a design review. If the triage questionnaire lives in the pull request template instead of the design template, the expensive decisions (which vendor, where the data lives) are already made.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Security champions, bug bounties and disclosure programmes
md: Champions scale security inside; a VDP with safe harbour invites help from outside. Both fail without the basics: someone answers the reports, and fixes have owners and deadlines.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Why a crash needs both undo and redo
md: Steal creates the need for **undo**, no-force creates the need for **redo**. ARIES allows both, so it must do both, using only the log and a little state stored on each page.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Four ways to tell the model which side a text is on
md: All four designs encode the same idea: one shared vector space, two roles. Use the exact pair (prefixes, instructions or input types) that the model was trained with, on the side it was trained for.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Batch jobs, idempotent pipelines and putting it together
md: Order of checks for each call: cache first (free, instant), then dedupe in-flight duplicates, then a concurrency limit and a rate limiter, then the API with bounded jittered retries. Anything that is not latency-sensitive goes to a batch job. Every side effect is keyed so that re-running the job is safe.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Compare-and-swap: write only if nothing changed, else retry
md: CAS turns "read, compute, write" into "read, compute, write *only if what I read is still there*". The retry loop is the general recipe: load, compute from the loaded value, CAS, and on failure recompute from the value CAS returned.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Zero-shot classification with CLAP audio and text embeddings
md: Choosing an approach: use a pretrained tagger's scores directly when AudioSet classes cover your needs; train a small head on frozen embeddings when you have a few hundred labeled clips; fine-tune when you have more data and compute; use CLAP-style zero-shot when labels change often or you have no labeled audio, and expect lower accuracy than a supervised head on the same classes.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Online attacks: brute force, credential stuffing, password spraying
md: Brute force is one account, many passwords. Credential stuffing is many leaked pairs. Spraying is one password, many accounts. MFA and breached-password checks defeat all three; detection needs counts across accounts, not just per account.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Why research needs a loop, not one retrieval
md: A research agent is not a bigger retrieval call. It is a harness loop whose next query depends on what the last read revealed, and whose output is a set of claims each tied to a source.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: On-demand capacity: tokens per minute and the max_tokens trap
md: Set `max_tokens` close to the longest answer you really need. The AWS docs say it directly: if you hit TPM quotas earlier than expected, reduce max_tokens to better approximate your completions. Measure real output lengths from the `OutputTokenCount` metric that Bedrock publishes to CloudWatch, the AWS monitoring service.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Running ternary models fast: I2_S, lookup tables, real numbers
md: bitnet.cpp's kernels are **lossless**: they reproduce the training-time quantization exactly. On 1,000 prompts with a 700M BitNet b1.58 model, I2_S, TL1 and TL2 matched an FP32 reference token for token 100% of the time, versus 1.4% for llama.cpp's own ternary formats TQ1_0 and TQ2_0, which quantize activations in 256-element blocks unlike training.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: When branchless loses, and how to measure it
md: Agner Fog's rule of thumb: a conditional jump beats a conditional move when the code is part of a dependency chain and prediction is better than about 75 percent. For random binary-search keys (about 50 percent) cmov wins; for keys that cluster, the branch wins.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Choosing an engine: tradeoffs, write stalls and failure modes
md: No engine minimizes read, write and space amplification at once. B+trees pay on random writes. Leveled LSMs pay in rewrites. Tiered LSMs pay in reads and temporary space. Pick the cost your workload can afford, then tune T, Bloom bits and compaction bandwidth.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Patches: run the big model once per group of bytes
md: A patch is a group of bytes that the big model treats as one position, with no fixed vocabulary. Average patch size sets the compute: forward cost per byte is about $2(m_g/P + m_\ell)$.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: unsafe: five extra powers, same borrow checker
md: `unsafe` does not change the rules; it changes who checks them. Rust programs must never cause undefined behavior, inside or outside unsafe blocks. Inside, the proof obligation moves from the compiler to you.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Where a line may live: sets, ways and tags
md: Power-of-two strides are a trap. In this L1d every address 4096 bytes apart maps to the same set, and a set has only 8 ways. Walking a column of `double m[N][512]` (rows of exactly 4 KB) puts every line in one set: only 8 of them can be cached at once even though the cache holds 512 lines.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Validating a graph with interventions
md: Graph first, intervention second. The graph proposes which features matter and how; perturbing those features in the real model is what turns a picture into evidence. Expect directional agreement, not exact numbers.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Estimating propensities: swaps, EM, harvesting, dual learning
md: Pick the propensity source by how much user disruption you can afford: randomization or swaps are simplest and most trustworthy, EM and intervention harvesting use existing logs but rest on model assumptions, and DLA learns everything jointly. Every option inherits the click model's assumptions; if users behave like a cascade, a position-only propensity is misspecified.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Browser extensions: someone else's code in every page
md: Nothing on facebook.com was vulnerable in that case. An extension with access to a site is effectively a trusted script on that site. For a site owner this risk sits outside your perimeter; for an organisation that manages its employees' browsers, it is squarely inside it.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: The shared responsibility model, and when the provider gets it wrong
md: Common misconception: "we are on a big cloud, so the provider handles security." The provider secures its platform. Your identities, keys, data and configuration are yours, and even provider-side bugs usually ended with a customer to-do: regenerate keys after ChaosDB, update agents after OMIGOD.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Logging and detection: what key abuse looks like in CloudTrail
md: Log everything that changes configuration, keep it in a place attackers cannot reach, turn on data events for buckets that hold sensitive data, and alert on a short list of high-signal events: logging disabled, root use, new access keys and users, policy changes, and known credentials used from new places.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Why analytic scans want columns, not rows
md: Columns win when queries read few columns of many rows; rows win for point reads and frequent updates of whole records. The layout decides how many bytes a scan must move.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization
md: Misconception: the `inline` keyword forces inlining. It is a hint plus linkage rules: rules about how the function's definition is shared between files. At -O2 the compiler inlines functions you never marked, and may refuse ones you did. At -O0 GCC inlines nothing unless the function has `__attribute__((always_inline))`.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: The observe-act loop: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
md: A computer-use agent is an ordinary agent loop where the tool is "the computer" and the observation is a screenshot. The model proposes actions in screenshot pixel coordinates; the harness executes them, and is the only place you can enforce scaling, safety and verification.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: How loom takes over the scheduler and walks every schedule
md: loom only sees what goes through loom types. A `std::sync::Mutex` or a third-party lock inside your code still runs, but loom cannot schedule around it, so executions that are possible in reality are silently not modeled. Libraries you depend on need loom support too for full coverage.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: iCT, sCM, LCM and the other few-step distillers
md: Consistency models learn the end of the ODE trajectory, not its slope. The boundary condition anchors the chain at the data; adjacent-time agreement (from a teacher's ODE step or from the data itself) propagates it to high noise; extra steps re-noise and jump again to trade compute for quality.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: The hash ring: each key goes to the next node clockwise
md: Consistent hashing minimises *movement*. It does not by itself give *balance*. With one random token per node, arcs vary wildly in size, as the toy ring shows. The next lesson fixes that.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Why scheduling explodes, and what a constraint model is
md: A constraint solver separates **what** a solution is (the model) from **how** to find it (the search). You declare variables, domains and constraints; the solver chooses the order of guesses and the deductions. Adding a rule means adding one constraint, not rewriting a search loop.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: One kernel, many tenants: the container threat model
md: A container is a fenced process on a shared kernel. Threat-model it as "attacker has a shell in this process" and ask which credentials, network paths and kernel interfaces that shell can touch.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: The API server is the front door: authn, authz, admission
md: Every request passes authentication (401 if unknown), authorization (403 if not allowed), then admission (mutate, then validate) before etcd. Reads skip admission, so RBAC alone protects them. Turn on audit logging, because it is off unless you configure it.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Network policies: from default allow to default deny
md: Pods are non-isolated until a policy selects them. Start each namespace with default deny for both directions, add DNS, then add one allow per intended connection, on both sides.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a hardening map and where to practise
md: No single control holds. Minimal signed images, Restricted pods, least-privilege RBAC, default-deny networks, encrypted and narrowly readable Secrets, authenticated node APIs, patched runtimes, and two kinds of detection: each covers what the others miss.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
md: Do not ask the LLM to copy job ids out of text. Give it the shown list with positions and attributes and let it output a position or an attribute match; code does the lookup. A model that types ids can produce a well-formed id that was never shown.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Do reasoning models admit the hints they use?
md: When the model can act on information without reasoning about it, its CoT usually stays silent about it, even with no pressure to hide. CoT monitoring then helps you notice frequent behaviors, but it cannot certify that a behavior is absent.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
md: A cross-encoder is not a better embedding model. It has no vector output you could store in a vector database. If someone asks you to index a corpus with a reranker, the answer is that you cannot: the score exists only for a specific query.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: What cryptography promises, and to whom
md: Ask of every design: which of confidentiality, integrity and authenticity do I need, against whom, and where does the key live? A primitive that gives one goal never silently gives the others.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Randomness: where keys come from, and the Debian disaster
md: A random-looking output says nothing about its entropy. Debian's weak keys passed every visual check; their weakness was only visible by counting how many could exist.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: From MMA atoms to TiledMMA and TiledCopy
md: Atoms are hardware facts, TiledMMA and TiledCopy are spatial arrangements of atoms, and partition_A/B/C or partition_S/D (source and destination) turn a tile into per-thread fragments. Swapping the atom (FMA, mma.sync, wgmma) changes the instruction without rewriting the loops.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Worked example: what a CXL access costs
md: Do not assume every CXL device behaves like Pond's model. Sun et al. measured three real devices: one had load latency only 35% longer than a remote-socket DDR5 node, while the other two were about 2x and 3x longer. Their bandwidth efficiency also differed widely by controller. Emulating CXL with a remote NUMA socket, as early research did, can mislead in both directions.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Why a loop over objects wastes most of each cache line
md: Memory moves in cache lines. Lay out data so that the bytes a hot loop needs are packed together, and the bytes it skips live somewhere else.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Testing equivalence: bitwise, tolerance and the cache-hit test
md: Determinism is not one property. Pin the reduction order and you get run-to-run equality. Pin it independently of batch size and position and you get the property a server actually needs. Keep RNG state per request and you get reproducible sampling. Test each one with its own experiment, compare at the logit level, and either go bitwise or attach a measurement to your tolerance.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Training: a weighted average of masked-LM losses
md: Perplexities reported for diffusion LMs are usually upper bounds (written as a less-or-equal sign in the papers), not exact values. Comparing a bound to an autoregressive model's exact perplexity slightly favours the autoregressive model.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Moving the KV cache: bytes, links and overlap
md: Overlap hides latency, not bandwidth. If two prefill GPUs share that 25 Gb/s link and each finishes an 8K prompt every 1.45 s, they produce about 1.4 caches/s against a link that sustains about 1.5. Add a third and the link becomes the bottleneck, however well transfers overlap.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
md: DPO swaps variables: instead of learning a reward and then the policy it implies, it learns the policy directly (the trainable $\pi_\theta$, with weights $\theta$) and reads the reward off it as $\hat r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$. This is the paper's subtitle: your language model is secretly a reward model.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
md: Until phase 4, at least one store is complete and current, and the other one is being kept in step with it. That is what makes every earlier step reversible. Plan each phase so it can be rolled out gradually (by percentage of objects or code paths) and rolled back with a flag.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
md: Move one thing at a time, keep one store complete until the very end, and measure agreement continuously. The deletion in phase 4 is the only step that should be hard to undo.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Affine quantization: storing reals as int8 plus a scale
md: Misconception: int8 means the model can only represent values between -128 and 127. The integers are codes; the scale maps them to any real range. What int8 limits is the number of distinct levels (256) inside that range, so the range you pick matters more than the bit width alone.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: L1: putting the token budget in the prompt
md: Length control needs an online reward that sees the generated length. The prompt carries the budget; the RL reward is what teaches the model to honor it.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Scoring a disaggregation: MAE, NEP, NDE and F1
md: Metric details change numbers silently. The on/off threshold (10 W in NILMTK) sets F1; whether a paper reports NEP, NDE or energy accuracy changes which appliances look good; and per-appliance averages weight a lamp and a kettle equally while energy accuracy is dominated by the kettle. Always state the metric definition alongside a number.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: From pairwise links to entities: clustering
md: Blocking decides which pairs are compared, scoring decides which pairs are linked, and clustering decides which records share an ID. Tune the threshold on labeled data, because it trades false merges against missed merges.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: The winner's curse: why the best public score is too high
md: The maximum of many noisy scores is biased upward. Selecting a system on a query set uses up that set: its score for the winner is no longer an unbiased estimate. The bias grows with the number of systems tried (roughly like sqrt(ln N)) and shrinks with more queries (like 1/sqrt(n)).

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Contamination: when test queries leak into training data
md: Putting it together: split by query cluster and time, tune on dev, read a sealed and rotating test set rarely, report paired bootstrap CIs, correct for every comparison you run, and check for contamination with fresh queries the model could not have seen.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Sandboxing as a layer: how Android hardened after Stagefright
md: A sandbox does not make a bug less exploitable; it makes successful exploitation worth less, and forces the attacker to find and chain another bug. Put the riskiest code (parsers of untrusted input) in the least privileged process.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: The setting: data that is not allowed to leave the device
md: The defining property is not cryptography. It is that **the data stays put and only parameters move**. In the standard description of the setting, a central orchestration server organizes the training but never sees raw data.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-gamma: expand every neighbor list by gamma
md: Misconception: "just raise M in HNSW". The paper notes that Qdrant's earlier densification idea did this, but $M$ also sets HNSW's level multiplier $m_L = 1/\ln M$, so raising it flattens the hierarchy, and HNSW is sensitive to its number of levels. ACORN keeps $M$ (and therefore $m_L$ and the level structure) fixed and expands the lists by $\gamma$ instead.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Online softmax: exact attention one block at a time
md: Online softmax is exact. The running max is only for numerical safety (keeping $e^x$ from overflowing); any consistent reference point gives the same $O/l$. Every FlashAttention version computes the same math; they differ only in how the work is mapped onto the hardware.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: The training target: straight lines and their velocity
md: The training loss does not go to zero even for a perfect network. Different pairs pass through the same $(x_t, t)$ with different targets, and a regression can only output their average. That average is the field you want, as lesson 3 shows.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: What 8 and 4 bits can hold: E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1
md: Exponent bits buy **range**, mantissa bits buy **precision**. E4M3 rounds with at most 6.25% relative error but spans only about 18 binades; E5M2 spans about 32 binades at 12.5%; E2M1 (FP4) spans 3.58 binades at up to 25%.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
md: Durable means: the bytes reached stable media **and** everything needed to find them (file size, block map, directory entry) did too. `write()` gives you neither; `fsync()` on the file and its directory gives you both.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing good harnesses: fast, deterministic and structure-aware
md: A harness that crashes on its own (a null pointer it should have checked, an `abort()` on documented bad input) floods you with false reports. Treat harness bugs as bugs: the fuzzer is only as trustworthy as the target function.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Symbolic and concolic execution: solving for the input
md: Symbolic execution is not magic search. It struggles with floating point, cryptographic hashes (a solver cannot invert SHA-256), huge loops and code it cannot see, such as system calls. Use it on the narrow, hard checks a fuzzer cannot pass, not as a replacement for fuzzing.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Transpositions and Indel: which edits count changes the answer
md: Two libraries that both say "Damerau-Levenshtein" can disagree, and "ratio" in RapidFuzz is Indel based, not Levenshtein based. When a threshold copied from one tool behaves oddly in another, check which distance and which normalization each uses.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
md: Quad code = coordinates of C and D in the frame where A is (0,0) and B is (1,1). Four numbers, independent of where the quad is, how it is turned, or how big it looks.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Better cells on the sphere: S2 cubes and H3 hexagons
md: H3 parent containment is only approximate. Seven hexagons cannot exactly tile a larger hexagon, so a child cell's area can stick out of its parent's boundary. The index hierarchy is exact logically (truncating an ID always gives the same parent), so aggregating by parent ID is consistent, but do not treat a parent's polygon as the exact union of its children.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Rounding, the small and large pools, and segment sizes
md: Every request is rounded to 512 bytes, routed by size (at most 1 MiB small, otherwise large), and served from a block in that pool. Only a miss touches the driver, with a 2 MiB, 20 MiB or rounded-to-2-MiB segment.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: From registers to HBM: the GPU memory map
md: Speed and capacity trade off at every level: registers and shared memory are on the SM and fast but small, L2 is shared by all SMs, and HBM is large but far away. Kernel design is mostly about making each byte fetched from HBM count.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Timeline first: where the 14.52 ms actually goes
md: The GPU utilization that Nsight Systems reports is **time** utilization, not resource utilization. Its own guide says so: a single running memcpy counts as the same amount of utilization as a huge kernel that takes over all the cores, and concurrent operations in the same chunk can add up to more than 100 percent. A 100 percent busy GPU can still be doing almost nothing useful.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: One kernel, many threads: grids, blocks and SMs
md: Blocks must not depend on each other. A thread may not wait for, or read results produced by, a thread in a different block of the same grid, because that block may not have been scheduled yet. (Thread block clusters, in lesson 4, are the one opt-in exception.)

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Finding communities: modularity and the Leiden algorithm
md: Communities come from edge structure alone. Leiden never reads a description; it only sees nodes and weighted edges. That is why the extraction quality from lesson 2 decides the quality of the topics.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: RLVR: replacing the reward model with a program
md: RLVR changes where the reward comes from, not the RL algorithm. Tulu 3 ran RLVR with PPO; DeepSeek ran it with GRPO. The rest of this course is about GRPO, the algorithm that made RLVR cheap at scale.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: GTFS Realtime messages and decoding them in Python
md: With FULL_DATASET, each fetch is the entire current state. If a trip's update was in the last message but is missing from this one, the consumer must treat it as having no realtime data now, and the reference is explicit that no TripUpdate does **not** mean the trip is on time.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: What a side channel is: secrets leaking through how code runs
md: A side-channel attack does not break the mathematics. It breaks the assumption that an implementation reveals only its outputs. Every defence in this course makes some byproduct independent of the secret, hides the secret from the computation that leaks, or keeps the observer away.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Hardware supply chain, coordinated disclosure, and practice
md: Hardware security in one sentence: the hardware runs your program correctly, but not invisibly. Keep secrets out of shared state (constant-time code, isolation, separate secure processors), keep firmware and microcode current, measure what booted, and expect new variants.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Choosing, verifying and debugging huge pages in production
md: Huge pages are a trade: TLB reach and shorter walks against contiguity, alignment and memory overhead. Use a hugetlbfs pool when you need certainty, THP in madvise mode when the hot regions are known, and check the counters, because both mechanisms fall back silently.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion: fusing by rank, not score
md: RRF is not parameter-free. Bruch, Gai and Ingber (TOIS 2023, ACM Transactions on Information Systems) gave each retriever its own k and showed that nDCG swings noticeably when those constants are changed, and that constants tuned in-domain did not transfer reliably out of domain. Also, the window size is a hidden parameter: a document at rank 11 with a window of 10 contributes nothing at all.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How a PLC thinks: the scan cycle and ladder logic
md: Changing a setpoint and changing the program are different. Setpoints are data the program reads (often over the network, by design, from the HMI). The program is the logic itself. Both can steer the process; defenders must watch and protect both.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Ukraine 2015 and Industroyer 2016
md: It is tempting to read 2015 as 'malware turned off the lights'. Investigators found BlackEnergy but could not show it played a role in the outage; people turned off the lights, through legitimate remote access. Monitoring that only looks for malware would have missed it.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Solving for a homography with the DLT, by hand
md: A homography maps points only after dividing by the third coordinate. Code that multiplies by H and keeps the first two entries silently computes the wrong point everywhere except where W happens to be 1.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: The IR lifecycle: NIST 800-61r3, CSF 2.0 and SANS PICERL
md: Rev. 3's main shift is not new phases but a new framing: IR is part of everyday cybersecurity risk management, and improvement is continuous rather than a meeting at the end.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Memory forensics: processes, connections and injected code
md: Memory answers "what is running right now and talking to whom", which disk forensics cannot. That is why memory is captured first and why rebooting a suspect machine before capture is so costly.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: SQL injection step by step: watching the query change
md: Removing the word OR, or blocking the quote character, is not a fix. It breaks real users (O'Brien, a shop in Portland OR) and misses inputs that need neither, such as a numeric field (lesson 6). The fix is to stop building SQL text out of input.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Submitting, waiting and how the kernel runs a request
md: Completions can arrive in **any order**. The ring preserves the order in which requests are *attempted*, not the order in which they *finish*. Always identify a CQE by its `user_data` (often a pointer to your per-request state), never by its position.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: tcmalloc: rseq per-CPU caches, spans and Temeraire
md: A restartable sequence must tolerate running its prefix many times, so everything before the commit must be side-effect free or harmless to repeat. Writing slot 5 twice is harmless here only because nothing reads beyond `current`.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Why the winner changes when the shape changes
md: A configuration is only ever best **for a shape on a device**. That is why the tuning result has to be stored under a key that contains the shape, and why `triton.autotune` takes `key=['M', 'N', 'K']`: the docs say a change in those values triggers evaluation of all provided configs.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Scaling across cores: one queue per core, rings and mempools
md: Scaling rule for bypass stacks: **one queue, one owner**. Hardware queues give each core a private path to the device, mempool caches give it private buffers, and rings or messages are the only places cores meet, always in bursts.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Limits of fusion and how compilers decide
md: A fusion is worth it when it removes HBM round trips or launches without blowing the on-chip budget or recomputing expensive work. Compilers estimate bytes saved, check legality, and fuse greedily; in training they also choose between saving and recomputing activations.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size
md: KV bytes scale with layers x KV heads x head size x bytes per value x tokens x batch. Weights are paid once; the cache is paid per token per request, so at long context and large batch it dominates.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
md: Eviction trades exactness for a fixed memory budget. Keep the sink tokens, keep recent tokens, and use accumulated attention to keep the heavy hitters; anything evicted cannot be recovered.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Finding a prefix across tiers, requests and engines
md: A cached block after a gap is useless for this request. KV at position 7 depends on every earlier token through attention in every layer, so if block 6 must be recomputed, block 7 must be too, even if an identical hash for it were stored. Eviction that removes a middle block silently strands everything after it.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Hybrid logical clocks: Lamport order that stays near real time
md: HLC is still one-way like Lamport: $(l, c)$ ordering never tells you two events are concurrent. Its gain is closeness to real time and constant size, not concurrency detection.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: ColPali: late interaction over page images
md: ColBERT and ColPali are the same idea at different granularities: keep one vector per token or patch, precompute the document side, and let each query token pick its best match.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Pause tokens, filler dots, recurrent depth and Coconut's costs
md: Loss of auditability is a design cost, not a detail. Latent thoughts can be probed with the LM head, but there is no readable trace to check. Pfau et al. raise the same concern: hidden computation can drift away from anything a human, or a behavior-based safety check, can read.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: PGM-index: guaranteed error with optimal linear segments
md: Pick epsilon, get a guarantee. The PGM-index fixes the last-mile search to 2 epsilon + 1 slots per level, uses the fewest segments that can meet that bound, and so its space adapts to how regular the data is.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: RankNet: a probability for every pair
md: RankNet does not need graded labels, only a set of preferred pairs. Burges notes the pairs can even be inconsistent, for example from a confused judge who prefers U1 to U2, U2 to U3 and U3 to U1.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The delta rule: overwrite instead of add
md: Forgetting to normalize keys is a real bug, not a detail. Take $k_C$ scaled to length 2 and $\beta=1$: the eigenvalue is $1-4=-3$, so a component along that key is multiplied by -3, 9, -27, 81, -243 over five repeated writes.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Processes, PIDs, process trees and signals
md: Read processes as a tree. Who started a process (its parent, its user, its command line in `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`) usually tells you more than its name, because names are trivial to fake.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: What an intruder touches: persistence and where defenders look
md: Do not investigate a live compromise only with the compromised system's own tools if you can avoid it: an intruder with root can alter `ps`, `ls` or the logs. Cross-check with package verification, a trusted copy of the tools, or off-host data.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore, and where they fail
md: Overlap metrics measure closeness to a reference, not correctness. A fluent answer with one wrong fact can outscore a correct paraphrase. They also penalize outputs that are better than, but different from, the reference, which is common once a strong LLM writes the outputs.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Inside an inference server: one engine step at a time
md: The scheduler decides **what** runs each step, the KV cache manager decides whether it **fits**, and the executor just runs a forward pass over token ids and block tables. Almost every serving optimization in this course is a change to the first two.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption
md: Admission control is a bet about future output lengths. Reserve the worst case and you never preempt but waste memory; allocate on demand and you fit far more requests but need a preemption policy (latest arrival first, all of its blocks) and a recovery method (swap or recompute).

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Why hard constraints need filters, not similarity
md: The LLM never touches the documents. It only translates the query into a filter object. Exact enforcement is done by the search engine, which is cheap, deterministic and testable.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Calls and tokens per query for each method
md: Calls set the latency floor and the per-call overhead; tokens set the bill. Listwise minimizes calls, not tokens. PRP buys robustness to prompt order with 20 to 100 times more prompts than pointwise (220 to 1,100 times more than listwise) at k = 100.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pointwise: yes/no relevance and query likelihood
md: Both pointwise methods need token log-probabilities. Many chat APIs only return generated text, which is why the RankGPT authors could not run them on GPT-4. And because each passage is scored alone, the score must be comparable across passages (calibrated), which the PRP paper argues LLMs are not trained to provide.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: SIFT: keypoints across scale and a 128-number descriptor
md: A SIFT keypoint carries position, scale and orientation. The descriptor is computed in that local frame, which is why it survives zoom and rotation, and its 128 entries are L2-normalized and clipped for lighting robustness.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Treiber stack: one CAS on the top pointer
md: Pop reads `old->next` after loading `old` but before its CAS. If another thread pops `old` and frees it in that gap, the read touches freed memory. Worse, if the node is reused before the CAS, the CAS can still succeed with a stale `next`. That is the ABA problem, and it is the subject of the next lesson.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drain: a fixed-depth parse tree and a similarity threshold
md: The one thing to remember: Drain bounds the work per line to a fixed tree walk plus a comparison against the few groups in one leaf, which makes its cost $O(n)$ in the number of lines. It buys that speed with two assumptions, that same-template lines share a token count and that early tokens are constants.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Normalisation: one event, one shape (ECS and OCSF)
md: A Windows 4625 converted to ECS and an sshd failure converted to ECS look identical to a rule, which is the point, but also a risk: a mapping mistake (say, putting the target host into source.ip) now breaks every rule at once. Test mappings with sample events from each source, exactly like rules (lesson 11).

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Baselines, anomalies and UEBA: how Storm-0558 was caught
md: State's advantage was not a product; it was three years of studying normal mailbox access, which let a modest-looking event stand out. The CSRB notes that buying the logs alone would not have been enough: few organisations analysed that voluminous log in detail.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Attention memory and Ring Attention
md: Ring Attention is not an approximation like sparse attention (each query sees only a chosen subset of keys) or sliding-window attention (each query sees only a fixed window of recent tokens). Each query still attends to every key; only the *order* and *location* of the work change. It also does not reduce FLOPs: total compute is the same quadratic amount, just spread over more chips.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Recurrent depth at scale: prelude, core block and coda
md: A looped model can quietly stop using its loop. If it learns to ignore $\mathbf{s}$, extra iterations do nothing. Track validation loss at several iteration counts (Huginn tracked 1, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64) during training, not just at the default.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Counting parameters, choosing targets, merging for free inference
md: Merging has a price: a merged model serves one adapter. Hu et al. note it is not straightforward to batch requests for *different* adapters in one forward pass once A and B are folded into W. Serving many adapters at once needs the unmerged form, which is the subject of the multi-LoRA serving course.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Measuring forgetting: TOFU, MUSE and the forget-retain tradeoff
md: Unlearning is judged against the retrained model on two axes at once: forget metrics should match it (not undershoot it) and utility should stay near it. Under-unlearning and over-unlearning both leak that the data was there.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: The PE format: headers, sections and what imports reveal
md: Our benign hello.exe imports VirtualProtect and VirtualQuery even though main never calls them: the MinGW-w64 C runtime's startup code uses them. One 'suspicious' import proves nothing. Read imports as a combination, and check what the compiler's runtime adds.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Writing and testing YARA rules
md: A YARA rule is a hypothesis about what makes a family unique. The test set is the evidence. Keep the test files and expected results next to the rule, and rerun them on every change, just like unit tests.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Shortlist then rerank: adaptive retrieval and funnel search
md: The first stage must have high recall (it must not drop the right documents) and the last stage high precision (what it puts on top must be right). Matryoshka prefixes give a cheap high-recall first stage from the same vector the precise stage uses.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Free memory you cannot use: two kinds of fragmentation
md: Fragmentation is not a leak. In a leak, *live* data grows because the program forgets to free. With fragmentation, live data is flat while the *footprint* grows. Tell them apart by comparing the bytes the allocator says are allocated with the memory it holds: a leak raises both, fragmentation widens the gap.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Relaxed: one agreed history per variable, nothing more
md: Myth: "Relaxed writes may take ages to show up, and SeqCst makes them visible sooner." The memory model says nothing about timing at all, only about order. A stronger ordering does not make data travel faster; it may even slow your program down.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Epoch-based reclamation: free garbage two epochs later
md: Holding a guard is holding back everyone's garbage. Pinning across a blocking call, a lock wait or a long iteration stops the epoch from advancing for all threads. crossbeam provides `Guard::repin` to briefly unpin and pin again inside long loops; references loaded before the repin are no longer protected.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Where things live: code, static data, heap and stack
md: The bug class tells you how memory is misused; the region tells you what gets damaged. Stack overflows threaten return addresses, heap overflows threaten neighbouring objects and allocator data.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Why memory-safe languages remove whole bug classes
md: Memory-safe languages do not make programs bug-free, but they turn the bug classes of this course from silent corruption into compile errors or clean crashes. That is why about two thirds of severe bugs in big C and C++ codebases are memory bugs, and why new code is moving away from C and C++.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Measuring re-ID: rank-1, mAP, the Market-1501 protocol, re-ranking
md: Report mAP alongside rank-1, follow the cross-camera protocol, and compare methods only with the same tricks and the same re-ranking setting, because tricks alone can move rank-1 by about 7 points.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Miles in one picture: slime's loop built for frontier scale
md: Nearly every Miles feature in this course attacks one of two failure modes: GPUs waiting on each other (throughput), or the trainer computing gradients for something other than what was sampled (fidelity).

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: distillation, exact alignment and a 744B run
md: Read the case study's reward numbers the way the report does: the nine-step moving average rose from 0.438 to 0.556 over 100 steps, but one run on one task set cannot separate that from run-to-run variation, so it is an observation, not a measured improvement.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why per-head keys and values make the KV cache huge
md: Cache size per token is set by what you store per token per layer. MQA and GQA shrink it by sharing keys and values across heads. MLA's bet is different: store one small learned vector per token and let each head derive its own keys and values from it.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Batching different adapters: Punica's SGMV kernel
md: SGMV groups rows by adapter and runs all segments in one launch, so a batch can mix adapters while the base matmul stays shared. Its cost grows with the number of distinct adapters and their rank, because each one's weights must be read.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
md: Use multi-query when recall is the bottleneck because users word things differently from the corpus, and the next stage can absorb more candidates. Skip it for precise lookups, compound questions (decompose instead), tight latency budgets, and pipelines where a fixed reranker budget already decides the outcome. Measure end-to-end, not just first-stage recall.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Why lookahead helps, and where it does not
md: These are intuitions, not proofs. The paper itself titles this section 'Why does it work? Some speculation'. Treat them as reasons MTP could help, then check the experiments.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon: orthogonalize the momentum with a few matrix multiplies
md: Muon = SGD with momentum + a post-processing step that equalizes the singular values of each 2D update, done with 5 bf16 Newton-Schulz iterations. Memory: one buffer. Extra compute: under 1% of a typical LLM training step.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: The muP rules, layer by layer
md: Every piece is needed. Keeping $1/\sqrt{d}$ attention, using plain `torch.optim.Adam` instead of `MuAdam`, or forgetting to scale `d_ffn` along with `d_model` silently breaks transfer while the model still trains. Lesson 5 shows how to catch this.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Building a mutex on a futex: the three-state lock
md: A good futex mutex makes the uncontended path pure user space: one CAS to lock, one swap to unlock, zero system calls. The kernel is visited only when a thread really has to sleep, and unlock calls wake only if the word says someone might be sleeping.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Write skew: the bug that snapshot isolation lets through
md: Repeatable Read in PostgreSQL is not serializable. The docs warn that business rules enforced by transactions at this level are not likely to work correctly without explicit locks or the Serializable level.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Scoring whole sequences: transitions and Viterbi by hand
md: A CRF changes two things at once. At **training** time the loss is over whole sequences, so the model learns which label follows which. At **decoding** time Viterbi returns the best-scoring sequence rather than the best label at each position, so the output is a well-formed tag sequence by construction rather than by repair.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Why MD5 misses copies, and the average hash that does not
md: A perceptual hash finds copies of *the same picture*, not *pictures of the same thing*. Two different photos of the same dog get unrelated hashes. For semantic similarity you need learned embeddings: vectors that a trained neural network outputs for each image, placed so that images with similar content land close together (lesson 5 covers one built for copies).

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Colocated vs non-colocated generation, and how weights are refit
md: Colocated means no idle GPUs between phases but strictly sequential phases and careful memory handoffs; non-colocated means dedicated pools, a network refit (NCCL by default) and idle time unless you turn on async GRPO.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: SYN floods and SYN cookies
md: A SYN flood attacks memory, not bandwidth: a few packets per second can hold a backlog full. SYN cookies move the half-open state into the sequence number the client must echo, so spoofed SYNs cost the server almost nothing.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Ethernet frames and MAC addresses
md: A MAC address is not an identity. Operating systems let you change it, [Android](https://source.android.com/docs/core/connect/wifi-mac-randomization) uses a randomized address per Wi-Fi network by default since Android 10, and it never leaves the local link: routers replace it at every hop. "Allow only these MAC addresses" stops honest mistakes, not attackers.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Reading a packet capture like a defender
md: Captures contain other people's data: passwords, messages, cookies. Capture only on networks and machines you own or are explicitly authorised to monitor, keep the files protected, and delete them when done. Intercepting others' traffic without authorisation is illegal in most countries (the security basics course covers the law).

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Worked example: what placement costs in latency and bandwidth
md: Good NUMA placement does two things at once: it keeps misses local (latency) and it spreads traffic over every memory controller (bandwidth). Losing either one can cost more than the latency penalty alone suggests.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Removing duplicates: greedy NMS and DETR's set prediction
md: NMS is not learned and does not look at the image. It only sees boxes and scores. It cannot remove a confident false positive that overlaps nothing (B3), and in dense scenes it removes real objects that happen to overlap.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Object storage is a strange kind of disk
md: Object storage is cheap, durable and shared, which makes compute stateless. The price is high per-request latency and a per-request fee. Everything else follows from batching writes and caching reads to pay that price rarely.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Inside a classic histogram: buckets, cumulative counts, interpolation
md: A classic histogram quantile is an interpolation inside one bucket. Its error is bounded by that bucket's width and nothing else, so a percentile panel is only as good as the boundary you placed next to the value you care about.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Reading a line: CRNN features and CTC decoding
md: CTC adds a blank symbol and a collapse rule (merge repeats, then drop blanks). That lets a recognizer train from whole-line transcripts with no character positions, and the blank is what makes double letters possible.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Discretionary vs mandatory access control, and the LSM hooks
md: MAC limits damage; it does not remove bugs. The SELinux Notebook is blunt: SELinux "will not stop memory leaks or buffer over-runs" and "will not stop kernel vulnerabilities", though it may contain their effects. A policy also cannot stop anything it allows.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Secure boot, module signing and kernel hardening knobs
md: Secure boot proves *what* booted, not that it is bug-free. A signed but vulnerable bootloader or kernel is still trusted, and the Ubuntu docs point out that initrd images are not validated. Keep revocation and updates flowing, and do not disable `module.sig_enforce` or lockdown "temporarily" to load an unsigned driver.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
md: A green local run does not prove CI will pass. CI tests your change merged into the latest base branch, on a clean machine, often across several OS and Python versions. Read the workflow file to see what will actually run.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
md: Approve when the change makes the codebase better than it was, not when it matches what you would have written. There is no perfect code, only better code. The goal is continuous improvement.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them
md: A repository with no `CONTRIBUTING.md` in its file list may still have one. It can be in `.github/` or `docs/`, or inherited from the organization's `.github` repository, which never shows up in the repository's own files or clone. Use the link GitHub shows on the new issue or PR page.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Fork, clone and two remotes: origin and upstream
md: Fetch from `upstream`, push to `origin`. Remote-tracking branches like `upstream/main` are snapshots from your last fetch, not live views.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Sign-off, the DCO, and how your commits land upstream
md: `-s` adds a Signed-off-by trailer whose meaning the project defines (often the DCO). Read CONTRIBUTING to learn whether the project wants sign-offs, fixups squashed, and which merge method it uses.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by
md: A sign-off you add without reading the DCO is still a legal statement about provenance. Copying code you cannot trace (a gist without a license, generated output in a project that bans it) and signing off is exactly what the DCO exists to prevent.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Regression checks: perf bots and noise thresholds from history
md: Regression checks only work if noise is known. A bot learns each benchmark's normal spread from history and flags changes beyond it; you do the same by hand with repeated, interleaved runs and a test.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
md: "Same problem" means the *same* failure, not just any failure. If removing a line turns a `StatisticsError` into a `NameError`, you did not shrink the bug; you created a new one. Compare the exception type and message every time, not just whether something crashed.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Why a reviewer sends a big pull request back
md: Misconception: "small" means "tiny". Google's guide also says a change can be too small to understand: if you add a new API, include a use of it in the same change so reviewers can judge it.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
md: The block table is the whole trick: contiguous logical blocks, scattered physical blocks, allocation on demand. Waste is capped at one partly filled block per sequence.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Authorisation: scope, rules of engagement and permission
md: If something is not written in the scope, it is out of scope. When a new system appears mid-test (a subdomain, an extra address range), stop and get written approval to add it. PTES names scope creep as a common failure, especially during retesting.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Reporting: from finding to fix, and the retest
md: A finding is done when the client can understand it, verify it safely, fix the cause as well as the symptom, and see it marked closed after a retest.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: A profiling workflow, its costs and its blind spots
md: The workflow: record with a modest rate and working stacks, fold, filter, draw, read top edges, fix the widest plateau that you can change, then measure again.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: The persuasion levers every lure pulls
md: Misconception: "spotting bad grammar catches phishing". Spelling mistakes were never the core of a lure, and well-written messages are now easy to produce: the FBI's 2025 IC3 report notes businesses reported over USD 30 million in losses to BEC scams involving AI. Train on the levers and the process rules, not on typos.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Layered defences and the analyst workflow for a reported phish
md: The NCSC also warns that punishing people for clicking simulated phish erodes trust and stops them reporting real mistakes; it starts to resemble entrapment. Teach the levers and process rules (lesson 2), make reporting effortless, and celebrate reports.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Scoring poses with Object Keypoint Similarity
md: OKS is averaged per object over *labeled* keypoints, so a person with only 4 labeled points counts as much as one with 17. Also, persons too small to have keypoint labels are not evaluated, and at most 20 detections per image are scored. Comparing OKS numbers across datasets with different skeletons or sigmas is meaningless.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Latency versus bandwidth: two different walls
md: **The one thing to remember:** ask whether the next address is known before the current load finishes. If not, you are latency-bound and more bandwidth will not help. If yes, you are probably bandwidth-bound and the question becomes how many bytes you move.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Windows escalation 1: unquoted paths and weak service permissions
md: Run the path audit and the ACL audit together. An unquoted path with no writable folder before it is a hygiene fix; with one, it is a working escalation to SYSTEM.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Failure modes, evaluation, and why some labs skip PRMs
md: Do not judge a PRM only by best-of-N accuracy. That metric checks final answers, rewards PRMs that act like outcome models, and depends on which generator produced the samples. Check step-level error location (for example ProcessBench) on the distribution you will actually run it on.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Why billion-vector indexes need compressed codes
md: PQ builds an exponentially large codebook, $(k^*)^m$ centroids, out of $m$ tiny ones. Each vector costs $m \log_2 k^*$ bits no matter how many dimensions it has.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Managed prompt optimizers and a practical workflow
md: A rewrite produced without evaluation data is a hypothesis, not a result. Treat it like a candidate from a proposer: score it on your validation set against the current prompt before shipping.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Text versus bytes: what a computer actually stores
md: Text is characters, bytes are numbers. Decode at the edge of your program (when you read), work with `str` inside, and encode again only when you hash, send or write bytes.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Encodings: base64, hex and URL encoding, and why attackers use them
md: Never decode and then *run* what you decoded to see what it does. Decode to text, read it, and search it. Executing an unknown PowerShell or shell command, even in your own terminal, is how an analyst becomes the next victim. Use an isolated analysis sandbox if you truly need behaviour.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Relevance feedback: Rocchio, pseudo-relevance feedback and RM3
md: Feedback is only as good as its top k. When the first-pass top results are relevant, PRF finds words the user never typed; when they are off-topic, it amplifies the error. On MS MARCO dev, the query2doc paper reports BM25 MRR@10 18.4 against 15.8 for BM25 + RM3, while recall@1k rose slightly (85.7 to 86.4).

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: RaBitQ indexing: normalize, rotate randomly, keep the signs
md: The rotation does not make every vector quantize well on every draw. It makes the quality *random with a known distribution*, the same for every input direction. That is what turns "works on my dataset" into a guarantee that holds regardless of the data.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft safety: the election restriction and the Figure 8 trap
md: A Raft leader commits by counting replicas **only** for entries from its own current term. Older entries become committed indirectly, when a later current-term entry after them commits. Entries keep their original term number forever, which is why this rule is needed.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Query-document features: BM25 per field, coverage, proximity
md: Per-field BM25 features are not BM25F. BM25F (the subject of Elasticsearch's `combined_fields` query) merges term frequencies across fields before saturating. Separate per-field features saturate each field on its own and let the model weigh them. Both are useful; they are different numbers.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Three runs, seven verdicts: when metrics disagree
md: Disagreement between metrics is information, not noise. If binary metrics and exponential nDCG disagree, your system is trading coverage of relevant documents against putting the very best one first. Report at least one metric of each kind and say which user you care about.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Scaling RDMA: NIC caches, doorbells, timeouts and failure
md: In practice: register big pools on huge pages, keep the number of connected QPs bounded (share, or use UD for fan-out), batch posts behind one doorbell, inline small payloads, signal selectively, avoid hot atomics, and handle error completions by resetting or recreating the connection.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: From a sparse rating matrix to item-to-item recommendations
md: Treating a blank as a rating of 0 is a modelling choice, not a fact. It makes plain cosine reward items that are merely *rated by the same people*, whatever the ratings. In Sarwar et al.'s MovieLens experiments, adjusted cosine gave lower error (mean absolute error, the average size of the gap between predicted and true rating) than plain cosine or Pearson correlation.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Evaluating recommenders without fooling yourself
md: Split by time, exclude what the user already consumed, beat tuned simple baselines, and confirm with an online experiment.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Aggregation and sorting: running state, hash tables and spills
md: A GROUP BY result from a HashAggregate has no defined order. If you need sorted output, write ORDER BY; do not rely on the order you happened to see.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
md: Misconception: reward hacking means the RL algorithm is buggy. DeepMind's analysis points the other way: the behavior comes from misspecification, and a *better* optimizer is more likely to find an intricate loophole that a weaker one would miss. Stronger RL makes the specification matter more, not less.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Governance, risk and compliance: three jobs and who decides
md: Governance decides who decides. Risk management decides what is worth doing. Compliance proves to outsiders that you did what you are obliged to do. They overlap, but a company can be compliant and still badly governed, or well governed and still breached.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Security economics: how much to spend (the Gordon-Loeb model)
md: Gordon-Loeb's lessons for engineers: spend where a dollar reduces the most expected loss, not where the scariest weakness is; for the paper's broad families of breach functions the optimum is at most about 37 percent of expected loss; and making controls more effective beats making budgets bigger.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: One control, many frameworks: CIS Controls, HIPAA and the crosswalk
md: Do not run one programme per framework. Write each control once, build it to the strictest applicable requirement, map it to every framework it satisfies, and attach evidence that is collected automatically. Start from CIS IG1 if you have nothing; use the crosswalk to answer everyone else.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Cyber insurance: what it pays, what it asks, what it excludes
md: Insurance does not replace controls or accountability. Regulators still fine you, customers still leave, and a claim can fail if your application overstated your controls or the event falls under an exclusion. Treat the policy wording as a contract engineers should read: what counts as a covered event, which notice deadlines apply, which incident responders you must use.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
md: After new weights land, cached KV entries are wrong: they were computed by the old weights. SGLang's `update_weights_from_distributed` flushes the cache by default, and AReaL's interruptible workers discard KV caches and recompute them with the new weights before continuing unfinished sequences.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: One fault, 397 alerts: collapsing the storm
md: Dedup and grouping are lossless: they change how many notifications you receive, not what was observed. Inhibition and silences are lossy: they delete evidence from your view. Use the first two freely and the last two sparingly.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: How k shapes the curve 1/(k + r)
md: Do not confuse RRF's k with the k of k-nearest-neighbors. Azure AI Search's docs stress that the RRF constant is "entirely separate" from the k that sets how many neighbors a vector query returns. Elasticsearch names them `rank_constant` and `rank_window_size` to avoid the clash.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Locks and refcounts as types: Guard, Opaque and Arc
md: The pattern is always the same: an `unsafe` C protocol (lock and unlock, get and put, register and unregister) becomes a value whose constructor does the first half and whose `Drop` does the second. The type system then tracks the protocol for every caller.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Worked example: weighted vtime fairness in a few lines of BPF
md: Weighted fairness in sched_ext can be three lines: order a custom DSQ by vtime, charge `used x 100 / weight` in `stopping`, and cap how far behind a waking task's vtime may be. Everything else (CPU placement, preemption, latency boosts) is extra policy you choose to add.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Attack surface, and the Morris worm's four doors
md: Attack surface is everything an attacker can touch: services, features, trust relationships and people. The Morris worm used all four kinds at once. The cheapest defence is removing doors you do not need (a debug command in production, an unused service); the next is making each remaining door check its input.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The attack lifecycle: kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK
md: Real attacks do not walk the phases neatly in order. Attackers loop (discover, move, discover again), skip steps (a stolen password needs no weaponization), and run phases in parallel. Use the models as a vocabulary and a checklist, not a script.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: STaR and ReST-EM: sample, keep what is correct, fine-tune
md: Each STaR iteration fine-tunes the **original** pretrained model on the new dataset, not the previous checkpoint, to avoid overfitting.
