ReST-EM does the same and reports much better transfer to held-out tasks than continuing from the last iteration. The model improves through better data, not through stacked training runs.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Prompt compression: pruning tokens with a small language model
md: Compression has costs of its own. The compressor runs on the critical path of every request. The compressed text is hard for humans to read, which makes debugging and audits harder. Exact strings (code, JSON, numbers, IDs) can be damaged by token deletion. And question-aware compression produces a different context for every question, so that context can no longer be served from the provider's prefix cache.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Log4Shell: how logging a string ran code
md: Log4Shell is injection in a place nobody thought was an interpreter. Logging user input is normal and correct; the library silently treated part of that input as template syntax with network access. Recall the injection course: whenever data is evaluated, the evaluator is the attack surface.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Inside the server: three processes and an overlapped loop
md: Chunked prefill trades the long prompt's time to first token for bounded step size: lower peak activation memory (activations are the intermediate tensors a forward pass keeps, and they grow with the number of tokens in the pass) and, when decodes are mixed in, steadier token gaps for everyone else. It does not reduce total prefill work.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
md: CH trades a one-time preprocessing pass (contract nodes, add shortcuts) for tiny queries: two upward searches that meet at the most important node of the route, then shortcuts are unpacked back into original roads.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
md: Misconception: "wider vectors always mean proportionally faster code." Width is only the upper bound. Memory bandwidth, latency chains and loop overheads decide how much of it you actually get.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Why a general-purpose heap wastes memory
md: Allocators are not just faster or slower `malloc`s. Each design gives up a freedom (free in any order, any size, any type) and gets speed or lower fragmentation in return. Ask which freedom your workload can give up.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
md: "Disaggregated" here is about trainer versus rollout GPUs. It is unrelated to PD (prefill-decode) disaggregation (`--prefill-num-servers`), which puts SGLang's prefill (processing the whole prompt in one pass) and decode (generating one token at a time) on different servers, and it does not imply async training by itself.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Verdicts, severity and priority: true, false and benign positives
md: Using a rule's historical precision in priority has a trap: a rule that is usually wrong will sink to the bottom forever, including the one time it is right. Precision should make you fix the rule, not ignore it. Target's "malware.binary" alerts are the cautionary tale.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Pivoting, building a timeline, and mapping it to ATT&CK
md: Do not force-fit. If you cannot say which technique an event shows, write the plain fact and leave the ID out. A wrong mapping in a case note propagates into reports and detection gap analyses.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
md: Dead latents grow with width; fix them with resampling, encoder-equals-decoder-transpose init and an AuxK loss. Feature splitting means the dictionary you get depends on width, so a feature is always 'a feature at this resolution'.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: The semivariogram: measuring how similarity decays with distance
md: The variogram turns Tobler's law into numbers: how much readings disagree, on average, as a function of distance. Its nugget, sill and range are what kriging uses to decide weights.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution
md: Speculative sampling is exact in math, not bit for bit. Chen et al. note samples match the target 'within hardware numerics': different batching, kernels and random number streams change floating point results, so a fixed seed will not reproduce plain decoding token for token.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: CTC and wav2vec 2.0: training without frame-level alignments
md: Two families: CTC models (like wav2vec 2.0 fine-tuned) classify every frame and collapse the path, so output is tied to audio frames. Encoder-decoder models (like Whisper) generate text with a decoder that also acts as a language model, which buys punctuation and multitask prompts and brings language-model failure modes such as loops.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Walking an x86-64 page table, bit by bit
md: A miss does not always cost four DRAM reads. The page-table entries are ordinary data that can sit in the CPU caches, and Linux's page-table docs note that MMUs also keep page walk caches for upper levels. The four loads are the worst case of the structure, not a fixed latency.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Side effects and how to evaluate a steering vector
md: LLM judges are convenient but not neutral. CAA used GPT-4 to score open-ended answers from 1 to 10 and notes the scores are sensitive to the rubric's wording; they spot-checked against their own ratings. String-matching refusal detectors have the opposite problem: they catch "I'm sorry" but not a harmful reply, so Arditi et al. paired them with Llama Guard 2.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
md: End-to-end exactly-once needs three parts: a replayable source (Kafka offsets), consistent state (checkpoints), and an output that is transactional or idempotent (upsert by a deterministic key such as sensor and window). Duplicates created upstream, such as MQTT QoS 1 retries, must be removed by id.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Positional encoding, residuals and the full Transformer
md: A Transformer layer = attention (mix across positions) + FFN (transform each position), each wrapped in a residual connection and LayerNorm, with positional information added once at the input.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: BM25 in Lucene and Elasticsearch: fields, tuning, limits
md: BM25 only matches the terms you typed, after analysis. A document saying "low-cost airfare" scores 0 for cheap flights. Synonyms, stemming, query expansion (adding related terms to the query), or a dense retriever (a neural network maps query and documents to vectors, ranked by vector similarity) are needed for vocabulary mismatch, which is why many systems combine BM25 with vector search.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature and top-k
md: The model never stores the text it generated anywhere except in `idx`. There is no hidden memory across calls: anything older than `block_size` tokens is simply cropped away and cannot influence the next prediction.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: walking downhill and choosing the step size
md: The gradient gives the direction; the learning rate decides the distance. The largest stable learning rate is set by the **steepest** direction of the loss, while progress in the **shallowest** direction decides how long training takes.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
md: `set -e` is a safety net, not error handling. It misses failures inside functions called from conditions and in `&&` chains. For steps that matter, check explicitly: `if ! cp src dst; then echo 'copy failed' >&2; exit 1; fi`.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Inside a GPU: many small cores fed by one big memory
md: A GPU is a throughput machine. It hides slow memory by keeping many warps in flight, not by making any single access fast. Give it too little parallel work and the SMs sit idle.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Batching: sharing each weight read across many users
md: Bigger batches are not free for users: once the step leaves the flat region (math roof, or growing KV reads), every sequence's inter-token latency rises. A throughput number without a latency number hides this.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why memory is slow and how caches hide it
md: Performance is often decided by memory access patterns, not instruction counts. Touch memory sequentially, reuse data while it is still in cache, and keep hot data small.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward models: turning human comparisons into a score
md: The reward model learns only from differences. Its job is to rank responses to the same prompt, and its output is a log-odds score: a gap of 1 means about 73 percent preference.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
md: The base of the log in idf does not change the ranking: switching from log10 to ln multiplies every idf by the same constant (about 2.303), so every score scales equally. What does matter is the shape, for example whether tf is raw or sublinear.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
md: Off by one is the classic C bug: `for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) a[i] = 0;` writes a[n], one element past the end. The loop condition for an n-element array is `i < n`. Neither the compiler nor the CPU checks array bounds for you.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Moves, Copy and clone: why let s2 = s1 kills s1
md: A move is not a deep copy and not a pointer trick at run time. It is a shallow copy of the value's bytes **plus** a compile-time rule that the source is dead. The heap block never moves.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A vector is a list of numbers and an arrow at the same time
md: A vector is an ordered list of $n$ numbers and also an arrow in $n$-dimensional space. Addition and scaling act component by component; the norm is the arrow's length.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Where it shows up: linear layers, batches and attention scores
md: Linear layers are batched dot products ($XW^\top + b$). Attention scores are dot products between queries and keys ($QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}$). Similarity search is a matrix-vector product. Vectors, dot products and matrix multiplication cover all three.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Fighting overfitting: validation, weight decay, early stopping
md: Choose capacity and regularization by **validation** error, keep the test set for one final check. L2 weight decay shrinks weights every step; early stopping returns the parameters with the best validation error; more data shrinks the gap directly.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: CPU scheduling: turnaround time versus response time
md: No policy wins on every metric. SJF and STCF minimize average turnaround but give long waits before a job first runs; round robin gives fast response but stretches every job's completion. Choosing a scheduler means choosing which metric you care about.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayes' rule: why a 90 percent accurate test is often wrong
md: The classic mistake is confusing $P(E \mid H)$ with $P(H \mid E)$, called base rate neglect. It shows up in ML with a classifier on a rare class. Its **recall** is $P(\text{flagged} \mid \text{positive class})$, the sensitivity, and does not depend on the base rate; its **precision** is $P(\text{positive class} \mid \text{flagged})$, the posterior, and does. High recall can still come with mostly false alarms.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND
md: $C \approx 6ND$. For a fixed budget, parameters and tokens trade off one for one in ratio: double $N$ and you must halve $D$.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Average precision, MAP and MRR: one number for a whole ranking
md: A common bug: dividing by the number of relevant documents *retrieved* (4) instead of all relevant documents (5). That gives 0.642 instead of 0.513 and silently rewards systems that retrieve fewer relevant documents.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Training embeddings with in-batch negatives
md: In-batch negatives assume the other passages are wrong. If the batch holds two copies of the same passage, or two paraphrased questions, the loss pushes a correct answer away. sentence-transformers recommends the `NO_DUPLICATES` batch sampler, which never puts the same text twice in one batch, for this reason. Hard negatives mined automatically can also be unlabeled positives, so they need filtering.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Encoding new text: replay the merges in rank order
md: Encoding is **not** "find the longest matching token from the left" and not "pick the segmentation with fewest tokens". BPE applies merges greedily in the order they were learned. A different procedure over the same vocabulary can give a different split, and the model was trained on BPE's split.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: A debugging recipe: loss at init, overfit one batch, read the curves
md: Every check has a **known right answer**: loss at init equals $\ln C$, one batch overfits to about zero, the real model beats an input-independent baseline. Add one piece of complexity at a time and re-check, so when something breaks you know which change did it.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Dependencies and transitive trees: code you never chose
md: Misconception: "I only use five packages." You use five packages plus everything they pull in. Count with `npm ls --all | wc -l` or `pip list` inside a fresh virtual environment, and you will usually find one to two orders of magnitude more.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: SBOMs: an ingredients list you can query when the alarm rings
md: An SBOM is a claim about contents, only as complete as the tool that wrote it. It lists what is present, not whether any of it is malicious, and an SBOM made from source can miss what the build pulled in. Generate it from the built artifact, sign it, and keep it with the artifact.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What happens when your program calls write
md: Two traps in the convention. The 4th argument goes in `r10`, not `rcx` as in a normal C call, because the `syscall` instruction itself overwrites `rcx` with the return address. And after the call, `rcx` and `r11` are garbage from your point of view. Compilers know this; hand-written inline assembly must list them as clobbered.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Why the average hides the requests users remember
md: Report latency as a distribution: several percentiles (p50, p99, p99.9) plus the maximum, not a mean. The mean blends a few terrible requests into many good ones and describes no actual user.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Allen relations, current roles and time-scoped queries
md: Every time-scoped question becomes interval arithmetic once two things are fixed: the reference date, and the convention for partial dates. Allen relations, current-role tests and window clipping are all a few endpoint comparisons.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation
md: The best use of test-time compute depends on the prompt. Search is most valuable where the model is weak but not hopeless; on easy prompts it can hurt by exploiting the verifier.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Wiring learned memory into real models, and what it costs
md: Common failure modes: (1) Wall-clock, not FLOPs, is the bottleneck. The TTT paper reports that TTT-MLP still faces challenges in memory I/O, and Titans' throughput falls roughly linearly with memory depth. (2) Inner learning rates that are too large make the memory diverge (lesson 2). (3) Without forgetting, a fixed-size memory overflows on long inputs. (4) Most published comparisons use models under 1.5B parameters.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Assets and adversaries: what is worth taking, and by whom
md: Do not let one view take over. The Threat Modeling Manifesto lists *tendency to overfocus* as an anti-pattern: avoid exaggerating attention on adversaries, assets, or techniques. A model built only around a feared attacker misses dull, likely failures.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Case: Target 2013, a vendor login across a trust boundary
md: Compliance is not security. The Senate timeline notes that Target was certified compliant with PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, the card industry's security rules) in September 2013, two months before the breach. An audit checks controls at a moment; a threat model asks how an attacker would get from here to there.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Forecasting is supervised learning where the future is off limits
md: A random train/test split on a time series leaks the future into training and makes every model look better than it will be in production. Hyndman and Athanasopoulos state the rule plainly: the training set may contain only observations that occurred before the test observations, so no future observations are used to construct the forecast.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Downgrade attacks: POODLE, BEAST, Logjam and the fixes
md: Downgrade defence has two halves: **authenticate the negotiation** (transcript signatures, the sentinel, SCSV) and **delete the weak options** so there is nothing to downgrade to. The second is the one that always works.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: From threads to blocks: the Triton programming model
md: A Triton program instance is not one thread. It is closer to a CUDA thread block: one program becomes `num_warps` warps of 32 threads each, so with the default `num_warps=4` a single program runs on 128 threads.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Attention masks for mixed text and image sequences
md: The rule that keeps any mask honest: a position may only attend to what will exist when it is generated. Bidirectional attention inside an image is legal exactly when the whole image is produced together, as in diffusion, flow or masked prediction. Under token-by-token generation it would leak the answer.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Syscalls become function calls: one address space, one privilege level
md: Running an unmodified binary on a unikernel does not get you function-call costs. Trapping and translating each `syscall` cost 84 cycles in Unikraft's measurement, 21 times a function call. Relinking against the libOS is what removes the crossing.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Graph traversal: memory layout, cache misses and prefetching
md: Deleting from hnswlib with `markDelete` only sets a flag. The node keeps its edges and is still used for routing; it is just filtered out of results. Lots of deletions therefore still cost traversal time until the index is rebuilt.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: 3D-HybridEngine: resharding the actor with zero redundancy
md: The paper describes the mechanism; today's code path is different in detail. With `actor_rollout_ref.hybrid_engine: true`, verl colocates actor and rollout, and the rollout is a vLLM or SGLang server with its own TP. After generation it sleeps (frees KV cache and weights); `update_weights` then wakes the weight memory, streams parameters tensor by tensor from the training engine, and finally restores the KV cache.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Tokenizing video and attending in space, then in time
md: In an ST-transformer the dominant cost, spatial attention, scales **linearly** with the number of frames instead of quadratically. That is what lets Genie use spatiotemporal context in the tokenizer, the latent action model and the dynamics model.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: The recipe: schedule, augmentation, per-layer learning rates
md: Augmentation is a training-time tool. At evaluation use only the checkpoint's deterministic resize, center crop and normalization; random crops or Mixup at test time just add noise to your accuracy estimate.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Why a transformer wants an image as a few discrete tokens
md: A visual tokenizer is to images what BPE is to text: a fixed map from raw input to a short sequence of ids from a finite vocabulary. Unlike BPE it is a learned, lossy neural network, so its reconstruction quality caps how good generated images can look.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: How vLLM chooses a backend: priority lists and validation
md: Automatic selection takes the first backend in the platform's priority list that passes `validate_configuration`. Explicit selection validates one backend and fails loudly. Neither path guesses.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Small text needs pixels: AnyRes tiling and dynamic resolution
md: Resolution is the main lever for reading text. Fixed-size models downscale, AnyRes adds tiles up to a grid limit, and dynamic-resolution models spend tokens in proportion to pixels. In every case more legible pixels means more visual tokens.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Consensus numbers: which primitives can build wait-free objects
md: The hierarchy is about deterministic wait-free algorithms. Herlihy notes that if the guarantee may be probabilistic (finite *expected* steps), the hierarchy collapses: randomized consensus from atomic registers exists. And a high consensus number says nothing about speed; it only says what is possible.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Scoring a forecast: latitude-weighted RMSE and ACC
md: RMSE rewards hedging. A smooth forecast that predicts the average of possible futures can beat a sharp, realistic one on RMSE while looking nothing like real weather. Read RMSE wins alongside ACC, spectra (how much variation a field has at each spatial scale; a blurry forecast is missing the small scales) or probabilistic scores.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Cookie attributes: Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Domain, Path, prefixes
md: HttpOnly is often oversold. It stops cookie **theft** by script, so an attacker cannot carry the session to their own machine. It does not stop script running in your page from **using** the session right there, which is what the Samy worm did. XSS still needs to be prevented at its source.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: PowerShell: objects in a pipeline, and why attackers like it
md: Misconception: "execution policy stops malicious PowerShell". It does not. Treat it as a seat belt for honest users, and rely on logging, AMSI and application control for security.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: WEP: how a 24-bit IV broke Wi-Fi's first encryption
md: A longer WEP key does not help. SP 800-97: the technique "has known flaws that are not mitigated by longer keys". The problems are the tiny IV, the linear checksum and RC4's key schedule, none of which depend on key length. If a device only supports WEP, treat its traffic as unencrypted and isolate it.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Android: UID sandbox, SELinux, verified boot and Play Protect
md: Rooting a phone (gaining root, Unix's all-powerful user) or unlocking its bootloader deliberately removes layers described here: verified boot no longer vouches for the system, and root can override the UID sandbox. Fine for a lab device, a serious risk on one that holds work data; device management and attestation checks such as the Play Integrity API (lesson 16) let organisations detect it.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Production run queues: fixed rings, steal half, a LIFO slot
md: Tokio's local queue is FIFO, not LIFO: the owner pops from the same end thieves steal from. For servers made of many independent tasks, fairness (no task waits forever behind newer ones) matters more than depth-first order. Locality comes from the LIFO slot instead, which Tokio uses at most 3 times in a row to prevent two tasks from starving the queue by waking each other.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: sendfile: from the page cache straight to the socket
md: sendfile shares page cache pages with the network stack. The man page warns that the transferred part of the file must stay unmodified until the reader on the other end has consumed it. If another process rewrites the file mid-send, the bytes on the wire can be a mix of old and new.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Prompting an LLM and calibrating its label bias
md: Two details. First, the bars show W p renormalized to sum to 1 for readability; the paper writes softmax(W p + b), which gives different numbers (T2 sports 0.911) but the same argmax, and the paper predicts with the argmax. Second, the bias is contextual: change the instruction, the examples, or their order, and p_cf must be measured again.
